definition: A test that is named for, or claimed by a document to hold, a behaviour still passes when that behaviour is removed, because its setup, fixture data, fake or duplicated assertion makes the outcome hold either way; this wins over every other untested-* kind whenever such a test exists.

No test fails when an error, refusal, exception, non-success answer (4xx/5xx, rejected request, thrown fetch, shutdown cancellation) or malformed-response branch is removed or changed; use it over untested-rule whenever the unheld branch is a failure path, and over untested-concurrency-guard unless the branch exists only to guard timing.

No test holds a limit, threshold, ruled constant or default at its exact edge (the value just inside and just outside, a one-sided check, a time-zone day edge, a count past a formatting threshold), so an off-by-one or a changed constant passes; wins over untested-rule and untested-wiring when the gap is about a value's edge.

No test fails when a registration, configuration binding, options validation hook, framework setting or startup wiring is removed or altered; use it when the gap is in how the application is assembled rather than in a request's logic.

No test fails when a guard for timing or staleness is removed (a still-mounted or idle-router check, a per-record key, a cache drop or placeholder around a re-read, an in-flight flag, a transaction-scoped lock or single-statement write against overlapping requests); wins over untested-rule and untested-persistence-effect when the guarded condition is an ordering in time.

No test asserts what a write leaves in the database (every column written, nothing saved on refusal, an untouched related row, a restricted cascade, a policy refusing an insert, a re-run changing stored credentials), so only the response is held; use untested-concurrency-guard instead when the point is behaviour under overlapping requests.

Existing tests already reach the code but never assert a specific visible output it produces (a caption or sentence, an element attribute, a severity, a problem title, an alert variant, the absence of a line), so changing that output passes; use untested-rule instead when no test reaches the code path at all.

Any other required behaviour (a design rule, an ordering of checks, a case held for one sibling entity, method, page or list but not the others) has no test that fails when it breaks; this is the fallback test kind, used only when no more specific untested-* kind or vacuous-test applies.

Request or file input is accepted when it should be refused or normalised (control or invisible format characters, surrogates, a comma list read as an enum, digits coerced to a number, unchecked array entries, a misread cell format) or refused when it is valid, so the code acts on a value the sender did not mean; wins over failure-misreported when the root cause is the missing check at the boundary.

An options or settings validator accepts a value that makes the application throw, overflow or silently misbehave later, or refuses a value the design accepts; use input-validation-gap instead when the value comes from a request or uploaded file.

Two overlapping requests or operations produce a wrong result (check-then-act, lost or merged update, a correct action answered as failed, a deadlock or uniqueness race surfacing as an unhandled error); wins over failure-misreported and input-validation-gap whenever the failure needs the overlap to occur.

The client shows, keeps or submits data from an earlier read or an earlier page state after it has changed (a cached record used as the form's start, a dropped read leaving an old copy, a status not refreshed before the next action, a choice silently dropped on re-read); use concurrency-race instead when the wrong result is produced on the server.

A failure is caught too narrowly or too broadly, mapped to the wrong status or message, swallowed, misattributed, lets a later failure replace a result already shown, or leaks a resource on its path; use input-validation-gap or concurrency-race instead when those are the cause.

A script, CI step or deploy gate reads the wrong signal as success or failure (a status code or stderr output misread, an unchecked command result used as a path, any listener taken as its own server, a same-commit redeploy passing before the restart), so the gate reports a result that is not the check's own.

A grep, lint rule, contrast check or acceptance command misses cases it exists to catch, has no negative control proving each of its rules can fail, or lives only in a document that will be deleted, so the rule it enforces can regress with every check green; use gate-false-signal instead when the check runs but misreads its own outcome.

A code comment, doc comment or class summary no longer matches what the code does (behaviour changed, a new caller or contract added, a claim overstated), in source or test files; use doc-claim-untrue for files outside the source tree.

A durable document outside the source tree (decision record note, deployment or README guide, instruction file, OpenAPI contract) states as fact something the code, pipeline or measurement does not bear out; use doc-pointer-missing when the line is only stale because a later note did not point back to it.

A change updates one record or note but leaves an older line it affects without the cross-reference pointer the register's convention requires, so the documents state the item both ways; wins over doc-claim-untrue when adding the pointer alone would fix it.

A rule, constraint or measurement that the code depends on is recorded nowhere durable (only in a plan, task document or clarification that will be deleted, cited from code by reference to such a document, or omitted from the note that records the fix), so a later change can break it unknowingly.
A version number, changelog entry or release claim does not match what ships (a version named but not bumped, a shipped change with no entry, an entry claiming more than was built).

A plan or task document's own bookkeeping is wrong (a task marked done without the required runs recorded, implementation notes or a testing strategy left behind by later changes); use undocumented-constraint when the issue is that a lasting rule lives only there.

New code departs from a written convention or the pattern its adjacent code follows (duplicated logic or data instead of the shared helper, a different structure for the same case, file naming, dependency placement, styling rule, test isolation style), with no functional defect being the main complaint; use the defect kind instead when the departure causes wrong behaviour that the finding demonstrates.

The interface renders or behaves visibly wrong in the browser independent of data (a style selector that never matches, focus not moved where the design requires, an overlay left open across a breakpoint); use stale-client-state when the wrong display comes from old data.
